sense: someone who writes letters and keeps records for another

evidence: Cic. Att. 12.40.1: librum ut tuīs librāriīs daret (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short (s.v. scrība): librārius is the private secretary, scrība the public one. Its first sense is a copyist of books, and after Augustus also a bookseller, so the setting must show which is meant.

terms.gloss: a secretary, one who writes for his master
evidence: Suet. Caes. 74: ā manū servus (Lewis & Short, s.v. ab)
terms.comment: The household slave who wrote at his master’s dictation; ā manū esse, to be someone’s secretary. Traupman gives it for a secretary, with āmanuēnsis.
Only in Suetonius (Lewis & Short), made from ā manū; the source of English amanuensis.

terms.gloss: a public clerk, a clerk to a magistrate
terms.comment: The salaried clerk of the Roman magistrates, who kept the public accounts and records (Lewis & Short): the word for the secretary of a council, a court or a society. In Christian Latin, a scribe of the Jewish law.

terms.gloss: a shorthand writer; a secretary who takes dictation

evidence: Suet. Claud. 28: Narcissum ab epistulīs (Lewis & Short, s.v. ab)
terms.comment: The title of the imperial secretary for letters; for a secretary who keeps the minutes, see scrība.
Traupman’s word, after the modern languages; it is not in Lewis & Short. For a government secretary of state, see minister.

phrases.latin: notārium vocō et quae fōrmāverim dictō
phrases.english: I call my secretary and dictate what I have composed
I dictated the letter to my secretary; it will go tomorrow.
